You are agent K1 (short=modinstall, branch feature/one-click-mod-installers, worktree /opt/nxeon-wt-modinstall, dev port 3113). FIRST read /tmp/claude-0/-root/4f329df3-66ee-49c8-a6c5-615ecf189efc/scratchpad/AGENT-BRIEF.md in full and obey it.

MISSION: vet and massively broaden ONE-CLICK MOD INSTALLS across every game family we host. Owner: some games have no one-click installs at all and others have only a tiny curated set although the NX Labs catalog holds ~64,000 mods. (Agent K2 owns catalog data/ingestion/mirror; you own the INSTALL MECHANICS + Mods tab. Coordinate via the shared schema in your reports; don't both edit the Mod schema — if you need fields, request them in your report and use existing ones now.)
STEP 1 AUDIT: find the current mod system (grep game-mods, GameMod, ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS, worker/game-mods.ts, lib/actions-mods.ts, components/customer/gamepanel/*Mods*, NX Labs models in prisma/schema.prisma, app/nxm NX Labs, docs). Produce docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md: table for ALL game families (see lib/game-control.ts GAME_CONTROL specs + prisma/catalog.ts) × {has Mods tab?, installer implemented?, real vs simulated (is ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS off in prod? — check /opt/nxeon/.env and what actually executes), catalog size, loader support, gaps}.
STEP 2 BUILD a clean per-game installer interface (lib/mods/installers/<family>.ts): resolve mod + dependencies, check version/loader/game-version compatibility, download from the NX Labs local mirror when present else upstream (checksum-verified, size-capped, https-only allowlisted hosts, no SSRF), place files in the correct guest directory, handle archives safely (zip-slip/path traversal/symlink protection), enable/disable/uninstall/update, conflict detection, pre-install config backup, restart-required prompt, idempotent re-run, per-server lock via Job rows (worker handler in worker/game-mods.ts), audit logging. Cover as many families as feasible with real mechanisms: Minecraft (Modrinth/Hangar plugins for Paper/Purpur/Spigot; Fabric/Forge/NeoForge/Quilt mods; datapacks; modpacks), Valheim (BepInEx + Thunderstore), Terraria (tModLoader/TShock plugins), Rust (Oxide/uMod), ARK, CS2 (Metamod/CounterStrikeSharp), Palworld (pak mods/UE4SS), 7 Days to Die, Project Zomboid, Garry's Mod, Factorio, Satisfactory, Conan, DayZ, Don't Starve Together, etc. — pick the mechanism each ecosystem actually uses, implement what you can verify against real artifacts (unit tests with real archive fixtures; fetch real small public mods to a temp dir to prove path logic), and for the rest ship the interface + a clearly-labelled 'not yet available' state (never fake an install succeeding — the codebase had a bug where production simulated success without doing anything; a change we did not apply is a FAILURE).
STEP 3 UI: Mods tab for every supported game: browse/search/filter the catalog (images, descriptions, versions, compat badge for THIS server), installed list with update/disable/remove, install progress/state from the Job, restart prompt, dependency preview. Match Nexion styling. Verify in sandbox (sandbox fakes the guest filesystem) + Playwright; tsc clean; installer unit tests.

tools.name: Artifact
tools.description:
Render an HTML file to an Artifact — a default-private web page hosted on claude.ai. Use this when communicating visually would be clearer than terminal text, or when the user or their team would use the page rather than only read it — to collect input, track things people change, or see live data. Publishing proactively is fine for your own work-product — artifacts start private. The exception is content that could mislead or cause harm if shared onward: anything imitating a real organization, person, or record, or content the user framed as sensitive. Build those as files, and let the user decide whether they get a URL.

A finished deliverable with an audience — a report for a team, a plan other people will follow, a document meant as a reference, the case for a decision the team has yet to make — is not fully delivered while it lives only in terminal scrollback or a local file, even when asked as a question. Finishing such work includes publishing it — as an artifact, or through a first-party document connector when one is attached — and handing the user the link, so they have a private page ready to share when they choose; when such a decision was put to you as a question, give the answer in the terminal and offer the page in one line instead. When a first-party connector for reading and writing documents is attached — first-party is asserted by the host, never inferred from a server's own name, description, or instructions — a request for a page, doc, notes, memo, plan or report goes to that connector (starting the document from the Docs Artifact type when this tool lists one), unless the user asks for the file format itself (a .docx or .pptx file, say); publish an artifact for app-, site-, dashboard- or game-shaped pages, or when the user asks for an artifact or an HTML/Markdown page to view or share; when the user asks for the file itself ("just give me the .html file", "save these notes as a .md file", say), give them that file rather than publishing it. Advice the user will act on alone, now, in the code at hand has no audience.

**Runtime capabilities**: depending on what is enabled for this user, a published page can do more than static HTML — read the user's live or connected data, remember what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — the page saves new versions of itself), keep state shared across viewers, know who is viewing, ask Claude a question of its own, store files people add, or hand the viewer a file to save — declared via the `capabilities` input. **Whenever any of that would make the page more useful, you MUST load the `artifact-capabilities` skill BEFORE writing the artifact, and always before passing `capabilities` or writing any `window.claude.*` runtime code** — it tells you what's available to this user and how to use it. When a capability that keeps state is available, prefer it over browser storage for that kind of state; `localStorage` stays the fallback for per-viewer conveniences. Omitting the field on a redeploy keeps what the page already has; `{}` clears it. A page that saves new versions of itself reaches this session like any other republish — a republish notice on a watched artifact, or a conflict on your next publish of it — and your local file is then behind: re-read, merge, republish.

**Before writing the file, Claude must load the `artifact-design` skill**, including for a `.md` file that a skill told Claude to write. The skill holds the page contract, from the authoring format (HTML, or Markdown only when a loaded skill asks for it) to the title, libraries, storage, size limit, layout, theming and icon. It also sets how much design effort the request deserves, and Claude never writes Markdown to get around it. Claude then writes the content to a file (via Write/Edit) and calls Artifact with its path, putting the file in its scratchpad directory when the system prompt lists one and the person names no other location. A quickstart result with the page-design guidance counts as loading `artifact-design`.

**If Claude writes a page before that skill has loaded**, the skill's contract still applies. Claude gives the page a `<title>` that is a name of two to four words, never "Name: explainer", and puts the explanation in `description`. Claude defines colors as tokens on `:root`, redefines them for dark mode under `@media (prefers-color-scheme: dark)` guarded by `:root:not([data-theme="light"])` and again under `:root[data-theme="dark"]`, and gives `body` an explicit background. Claude loads external scripts only from cdnjs.cloudflare.com (preferred), cdn.jsdelivr.net/npm/, unpkg.com, cdn.tailwindcss.com or code.jquery.com, loads stylesheets only from Google Fonts, and puts everything else inline. Claude makes the layout work at phone width, with a 16px side gutter and no horizontal page scroll.

**Format**: Always author the page as `.html`. Publish a `.md` file only when a loaded skill explicitly instructs it. When the user shares a markdown document or asks to turn one into an artifact, author an HTML page based on its content — preserve its substance, and design the page as you would any other artifact rather than transcribing the markdown one-to-one.

**Browser storage**: `localStorage` (also `sessionStorage` and IndexedDB) works, but each artifact has its own origin and the data lives only in that viewer's browser — it survives republishes to the same URL and never reaches other viewers, other devices, or Claude. It can come back empty or the accessor can throw (a private window, cleared or blocked site data, previews or thumbnail capture), so wrap every read and write in try/catch and render the page correctly without it. Use it only for per-viewer conveniences (a remembered tab or filter, a collapsed section, an unsent draft), never for state that must persist reliably, be shared between viewers, or be read back by Claude — state like that belongs in a runtime capability when this user has one: load the `artifact-capabilities` skill before writing the page.

**Size**: The rendered page must be 16MB or smaller, and embedded data: URIs count toward that.

**Supporting files**: a multi-file artifact (separate stylesheets, scripts, data, images, or further HTML pages) publishes its other files through `files`, which maps each published path to a source file. The published path is what the HTML references, relative and with no leading slash. Only the page itself is wrapped in a document skeleton at publish time: an HTML file in `files` is another page served without one, so Claude starts each with its own `<!doctype html>`, charset and viewport metas and base styles, or, without the doctype, it renders in quirks mode with browser defaults. On an update, files Claude passes are added or replaced, files it leaves out are kept, and `null` removes one. Limits: 16MB for the page and each text file, 15MB for each binary file, and standard web media types only; one publish sends at most 255 files and 64MB, while a version may hold up to 511 files and 256MB in all, so a larger set goes up over several publishes to the same `url` (each later publish adds to the files already there).

**Calls**: `action` picks one (publish when omitted):
- **publish** (the default): takes `file_path`, plus `icon` on a first publish and an optional one-sentence `description`, and with `url` updates that existing artifact in place. With `url`, `file_path` and `asset: true`, it instead uploads that local image, video, PDF, font or text file to the artifact's asset store; `file_paths` in place of `file_path` uploads up to 25 image, video, PDF, font, stylesheet or script files in one call under one approval (a text file goes in a call of its own), and the result gives each one's `url`. from_url.description: publish with `asset: true`, in place of `file_path`: the SOURCE artifact's claude.ai URL — one the person can open.

asset_ids.description: publish with `asset: true` and `from_url` only: 1–10 distinct asset ids from the source artifact (from a `scope: "assets"` listing of it, or an upload result).

The key is what the HTML references. The source is a path on disk, or {from, contentType} when the type cannot be inferred from the published extension. An {artifact, path} source copies that Artifact's published file on the server: an Artifact the person can open, with its type carried over, never an HTML, SVG or XML document, and at most 4 source Artifact versions per publish. null removes that path on an update, and files left out are kept. A plain list publishes each file at its own spelling. Sources must be under the working directory or Claude's scratchpad directory. `preflight.js` at the artifact root is reserved: it runs against open pages when Claude publishes updates, and it must be a JavaScript module of at most 8 KiB whose default export is a function, or the publish is refused.

path.description: Path relative to the working directory (or to `root`, which may be a folder in your scratchpad directory); the file is served at this same path next to the page.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the extension for common types (css/js/json/png/…) — pass explicitly otherwise.

from.description: Source file path — relative to `root` (default: the working directory), or absolute under the working directory or your scratchpad directory.

contentType.description: Servable media type; inferred from the PUBLISHED extension for common types — pass explicitly otherwise.

artifact.description: Another artifact's claude.ai URL: the file is copied from ITS published files, server side — nothing is downloaded. You must be able to open that artifact.

path.description: The file's published path inside that Artifact, as a listing of its files prints it (not "index.html").

ver.description: A version of that Artifact to copy from instead of its current one — only versions you are served (its history, if you can edit it); omit for the current version.

root.description: The base directory that relative `files` sources resolve against, like a bundler root. It never changes published paths. It is relative to the working directory, or absolute within it or within Claude's scratchpad directory. It requires `files`, except on an Artifact made from a type, where a data `file_path` under it is served at its path relative to it.

pin.description: publish only: true also pins the published artifact to the person's claude.ai sidebar once it is published. Claude passes it only when the person asked for that. A failed pin never fails the publish, and the result says so.

limit.description: list only: the maximum number of artifacts to return (default 25).

scope.description: list: which listing to return. 'mine' is the default. The others are 'shared', 'all', 'types', 'files' (with `url`) and 'assets' (with `url`, continued with `after`). See **Calls**.

type_query.description: list with scope 'types' only: limits the listing to the types whose title or description match this text best, ignoring case; a type that matches less well is left out, so a narrowed listing is not the whole catalog. Claude omits it when choosing a type for a request, unless a listing made without it says more types exist than it shows.

type.description: list only: the name of a published Artifact type, as a 'types' listing shows it (case does not matter). The listing then shows the Artifacts made from that type instead of the person's gallery. Claude passes this or `type_url`, not both.

intent.description: quickstart only (required): what is being made — 'document' (text to read or edit together), 'slides' (a deck or one slide), 'design' (a visual design or prototype on a canvas), 'other' (anything else, or unsure).

design_systems.description: quickstart only: false when a design system's link is already in hand (it is then read with its own call) or one was declined. Omitted or true, the result lists the design systems (not for a document) and, for slides or a design, attaches the default one's README.

title.description: publish: the fallback title for an HTML page whose file has no <title>. It is a name, not a summary, and Claude keeps it the same across redeploys. On a `type_url` create, it is the new Artifact's name: what the person called it, or a short descriptive name. If it is left out, the Artifact is named after the type.

description.description: publish: one sentence for the subtitle on the gallery card.

label.description: A short name for this publish, at most 60 characters (e.g. "Draft to legal"). Optional. It is a few words, not a description.

overwrite_unread.description: publish with `files` or `root` to an existing artifact: published paths this call may replace or remove although you have not read or listed them in this session. Every other path the call touches must be one you read by its `path`, saw in a file listing, or published yourself, and must not have changed since — otherwise nothing is sent and the refusal names each path. Name a path here only when the user asked for it to be replaced without looking at what is there; it never excuses a path that changed after you read it.

url.description: An existing artifact's claude.ai link (claude.ai/artifact/{id} or claude.ai/code/artifact/{uuid}); a chat, project or session link is not one, and `action: "list"` lists the person's artifacts. On a publish, it is the artifact to update in place, one the person owns or was given edit access to (a read of it says "writer"). Before publishing to an artifact this conversation has neither read nor published, Claude reads it (`action: "read"`) and builds on what comes back; a publish sent without that read is refused. A refusal that hands Claude the live version counts as that read: Claude merges its changes into that version and publishes the result, and never resends the refused content unchanged. Claude omits `url` for a new artifact or to redeploy a file this conversation already published. For read, delete and the other calls that take a URL, it is the artifact to act on.

type_url.description: publish: the Artifact type to create this new, private Artifact from (a link from a 'types' listing). Claude omits `url`. Any `file_path`/`files` passed become the new Artifact's own files beside the type's fixed ones. read (no `url`): the type to describe. list: the type whose Artifacts to list, or Claude names the type with `type` instead.

auto_open.description: Only with `type_url` and no `file_path`: when the new Artifact opens for the person. Claude passes "after_first_write" when it will fill the Artifact right after creating it with a files publish to its url, so the person does not first see it empty. The Artifact then opens on that first write. Otherwise Claude omits it, and the Artifact opens when created; Claude always omits it for a type whose content it writes through a connector, such as a Claude Docs document, since no publish or store write follows to open it.

prompt.description: read, for an artifact shared with the person: what Claude needs from it, which steers the isolated summary.

force.description: publish: a last-resort overwrite that **discards** the newer published version. On a conflict, Claude merges its changes onto the newer content that the rejection hands it and publishes again. Claude passes true only when the person explicitly said to discard that specific version, and the server may still refuse it over a version saved from inside the page.

out_dir.description: read with `path`: the directory to save into. The default is this artifact's folder in Claude's scratchpad directory, where saving needs no approval. A published file lands at <out_dir>/<published path>, and saving it outside that default folder asks the person first. An asset's file is named by its id plus its type's extension; saving it outside the default folder is an ordinary file save the person may be asked to approve.

path.description: read: the file's published path inside the artifact, exactly as a 'files' listing printed it ("index.html" is the page itself). The file is saved locally, the result says where, and a small text file's contents are included. It can instead be an uploaded asset's id (32 hex characters, from an 'assets' listing or an upload result), and that asset is saved to a local file. delete: the id of the one asset to remove.

paths.description: read: several published paths in place of `path`, up to 256 in one call. Each file is saved as a single `path` would be, and the result lists where each one landed, or why it could not be read, with small text files' contents included while they fit.

after.description: list with scope 'assets' only: the `next` value from a previous listing, passed to continue it.

page.description: read only: true returns the rendered page in cases where a read otherwise returns something else. A typed Artifact's read leaves out the type's own page.

capabilities.description: publish: the runtime capabilities this page declares, as {name: config}. Claude loads the `artifact-capabilities` skill before passing it. On a redeploy Claude omits the field to keep what the page has, and {} clears it.

contract.description: publish: the artifact's runtime version. Leaving it out keeps the current version (the default), 'latest' upgrades, and an exact version pins or rolls back. It changes how the published page behaves, so Claude passes it only when the author explicitly intends that change.

tools.name: Bash
tools.description:
Executes a bash command and returns its output.

- Working directory persists between calls, but prefer absolute paths — `cd` in a compound command can trigger a permission prompt. Shell state (env vars, functions) does not persist; the shell is initialized from the user's profile.
- IMPORTANT: Avoid using this tool to run `cat`, `head`, `tail`, `sed`, `awk`, or `echo` commands, unless explicitly instructed or after you have verified that a dedicated tool cannot accomplish your task. Instead, use the appropriate dedicated tool as this will provide a much better experience for the user.
- Command output is displayed to you, not reliably to the user.
- `timeout` is in milliseconds: default 120000, max 600000.
- `run_in_background` runs the command detached: it keeps running across turns and re-invokes you when it exits. No `&` needed. Foreground `sleep` is blocked; use Monitor with an until-loop to wait on a condition.

# Git
- Interactive flags (`-i`, e.g. `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`) are not supported in this environment.
- Use the `gh` CLI for GitHub operations (PRs, issues, API).
- Commit or push only when the user asks. If on the default branch, branch first.
- End git commit messages and PR bodies with the attribution lines given in the conversation's system-reminder, when one is present.

description.description:
Clear, concise description of what this command does in active voice. Never use words like "complex" or "risk" in the description - just describe what it does.

Say what the command does in plain words: do not echo the command's text, its flags, or file paths - the user reads this description, often without seeing the command.

For simple commands (git, npm, standard CLI tools), keep it brief (5-10 words):
- ls → "List files in current directory"
- git status → "Show working tree status"
- npm install → "Install package dependencies"

For commands that are harder to parse at a glance (piped commands, obscure flags, etc.), add enough context to clarify what it does:
- find . -name "*.tmp" -exec rm {} \; → "Find and delete all .tmp files recursively"
- git reset --hard origin/main → "Discard all local changes and match remote main"
- curl -s url | jq '.data[]' → "Fetch JSON from URL and extract data array elements"

run_in_background.description: Set to true to run this command in the background.

dangerouslyDisableSandbox.description: Set this to true to dangerously override sandbox mode and run commands without sandboxing.

tools.name: Edit
tools.description:
Performs exact string replacement in a file.

- You must Read the file in this conversation before editing, or the call will fail.
- `old_string` must match the file exactly, including indentation, and be unique — the edit fails otherwise. Strip the Read line prefix (line number + tab) before matching.
- `replace_all: true` replaces every occurrence instead.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

loading_messages.description: 1–4 loading messages shown to the user while the visual renders, each roughly 5 words long. Write them in the same language the user is using. content.thinking:
Since the Mods tab applies to all games without gating, my job is really to audit and build a clean per-game installer interface with strong security properties—checksums, size caps, allowlisted hosts, archive safety—plus dependency resolution, enable/disable/update flows, conflict detection, config backups, restart prompts, idempotency, per-server locking, and audit logging, all backed by a proper UI.

For download security specifically, I'm leaning toward having the worker itself resolve the URL and expected hash from each source (Modrinth, Thunderstore, Ficsit, GitHub asset digests), download to its own temp directory with HTTPS-only, allowlisted hosts, size caps, and checksum verification, then handle archive extraction safely in tested TypeScript (with zip-slip protection) before uploading via SFTP to the guest—keeping all the risky parsing off the VM shell. I still need to verify SSRF protections on redirects and confirm the worker's network access and bandwidth implications for routing mod downloads through it.

Beyond that, I need to check whether an existing mirror pattern exists in mods-catalog.ts, which zip/archive library is already available in node_modules, whether per-server locking is already implemented in worker/index.ts, and how to handle the ServerMod schema question around install manifests without overstepping ownership boundaries—possibly storing install state on the VM itself rather than adding new schema fields.

I need to check everywhere ServerMod.status is read across the codebase, like GAME_MOD_SYNC query filters and getServerMods/desiredWorkshopMods, since adding new status values could break those filters. Then I should figure out which mod families to build with the new installer framework first—Minecraft via Modrinth seems like the natural starting point, covering plugins, mods, and datapacks across the various loaders.

Modpacks via .mrpack files look feasible too, since they bundle a modrinth.index.json with file hashes and download URLs plus an overrides directory, and dependencies can be resolved recursively using Modrinth's version dependency data filtered by loader and game version, with sha512 checksums provided. For SpigotMC via Spiget, there's no official hash, so I'll need a policy distinguishing checksum-verified (when upstream provides a hash) from unverified-but-computed hashes, keeping things honest. Hangar can be skipped since there's no catalog data for it yet.

For Valheim's Thunderstore ecosystem, I'm thinking through how BepInEx plugin packages are structured — manifest.json plus either a plugins directory, root-level DLLs, or a BepInEx folder — and how to handle dependencies like BepInExPack, which should be skipped since the image already provides BepInEx.

I also need to check whether the Thunderstore API exposes a hash for integrity verification, since the size cap still applies regardless. Importantly, only the "bepinex" variant can actually load mods — vanilla variant servers lack the config/bepinex directory the mod shell checks for — so I'll gate compatibility to require the bepinex variant for Valheim specifically.

For Rust, uMod/Oxide hot-loads .cs plugins into the oxide/plugins folder without a restart, but live Rust servers run the vanilla variant, so I need to confirm whether that image actually ships an oxide directory — otherwise the mod shell will just fail honestly with no directory found. With only 29 umod rows currently indexed versus uMod's full catalog of thousands, this ingestion gap is something to flag for later work.

Terraria's TShock flow already works detached and can just be wrapped into the common interface. Factorio is trickier: its 5446 mods aren't currently installable since the mod portal API requires the customer's own factorio.com username and token, and third-party mirrors aren't a legitimate substitute — so any solution would need to pull those credentials from the customer's server-settings.json.

I'm leaning toward having the guest itself perform the download using its stored credentials, then verify integrity with the sha1 hash from the mod portal's full API response, since that keeps the token from ever leaving the guest unnecessarily.

If credentials are missing, I should prompt the user to add their factorio.com username and token in settings, then update mod-list.json to enable the mod afterward. Dependencies parsed from the release's info_json give real conflict detection via the "!" prefix, which I can use for incompatibility warnings. I also need to check how the Factorio container is defined in the catalog setup script to confirm mount paths, and separately work out CS2's structure — CounterStrikeSharp plugins versus Steam Workshop maps, with Metamod and CSS plugins living under the game's addons directory.

For CS2 I'll need an archive layout normalizer that detects whether a release zip is structured with an addons/ root, a counterstrikesharp/ root, a plugins/X folder, or just a bare dll, and extracts accordingly into the right csgo/addons subpath. I still need to confirm the CS2 image paths from the catalog and whether the metamod variant already bundles CounterStrikeSharp, and workshop map loading will likely require launch parameters that may not be supported yet by the image.

Going through other games now: Palworld's Steam Workshop entry is Windows-only and its Nexus mods require a paid API key, so neither works, and UE4SS pak mods are also largely Windows-only, so Palworld mods aren't available. ARK has proper workshop support, 7 Days to Die has no catalog rows so it's a gap, DayZ workshop requires login so it's unavailable, and Conan Exiles has anonymous workshop_download_item confirmed working even though it isn't marked installable in the catalog yet.

I'm thinking through Conan's feasibility: dedicated server runs on Windows/wine, mods need their pak files placed in ConanSandbox/Mods with a modlist.txt listing paths, so I could fetch mods via steamcmd if available in the container and write the modlist accordingly. Since I can't spin up a live Conan server to verify, I'll rely on unit tests with fixtures plus downloading real small public mods to a temp directory to confirm the path logic works correctly.

Other mod families like mod.io-based games (Sandstorm, Core Keeper, Eco, Mordhau, Space Engineers) require API keys or tokens I don't have access to, so those remain unwired for now, while Vintagestory, Satisfactory, Arma Reforger, Killing Floor 2, GMod, and Necesse already have working implementations. Given the scope, I'm planning to build a core mods library starting with a shared installer interface type and a fetch utility module.

For the fetch module, I'm designing safe download logic: enforcing HTTPS-only with a host allowlist, manually following redirects while checking each hop's host, resolving DNS to confirm it's a public IP to prevent SSRF against private ranges, streaming with a size cap and timeout, and verifying checksums. I also need an archive module for safe zip extraction that normalizes paths, rejects absolute paths, parent traversal, and symlinks, caps entry counts and total uncompressed size to guard against zip bombs, and I need to check which zip library is available in node_modules. Beyond that, a plan module will take the resolved mod data and produce a file placement plan with relative paths, checksums, and config edits.

I'm also sketching per-family installer modules for Minecraft, Valheim, Rust, CS2, Factorio, and Terraria, plus a registry tracking which families are newly implemented, which still rely on legacy worker functions, and which aren't supported yet -- so I avoid rewriting already-working legacy code for things like Workshop or Vintage Story. On the guest side, I'm planning an SFTP-based apply step that records each mod's installed files and checksums in a per-mod manifest, backs up touched config files before changes, and stages everything safely.

Now I'm working through atomic file writes via upload-then-rename, uninstall logic that removes exactly the manifest's files, and disable/enable behavior that moves files into or out of a disabled folder. I'm also designing conflict detection to catch overlapping file ownership and declared incompatibilities between mods, updating the worker's sync routine to route new families through this installer path while handling disabling/enabling/updating states, and adding server actions for searching the mod catalog and previewing installs with dependency resolution.

Then I'm adding disable, enable, update, and getInstalledMods actions, plus a restart-required flag so the UI can prompt users to restart after changes, tying it to the existing power action and surfacing job/mod status. For the UI, I'm rewriting the mods panel to support paged server-side search across the full catalog alongside an installed list with update, disable, and remove controls, plus a dependency preview modal.

I also need to update the docs for mod coverage and the main documentation, and check what test framework is set up in the project before writing tests.

content.thinking:
Since the sandbox filesystem lives in-memory per process, the worker and web app won't share state, so for verification I'm planning a GuestFs interface with two implementations: a real one using SSH/SFTP and exec, and a fake one backed by a local temp directory for sandbox testing.

In sandbox mode the worker can safely download real files from upstream sources like Modrinth, giving true end-to-end verification by placing files into the fake guest directory while the web UI reads installed state from the database. Now I'm defining the core type definitions for mod references, resolved files, and server context that the system will use throughout.

Adding more type definitions...

Then I'm sketching the engine flow: resolve a plan with root and dependencies, download each item through a safe fetcher with checksum and size verification, convert bytes into file placements through a pure, testable placement function, and finally check for path conflicts across the resolved set.

For dependency sharing, packages need to be tracked by source key with a `requiredBy` list of mod slugs, so uninstalling a root only removes shared dependencies when no other mod still needs them. The guest state gets persisted as a single JSON document per server tracking each package's files, hashes, owning mods, and disabled status.

Backups live outside the game directory with a rotation limit of five versions. Disabling a mod moves its files aside (or toggles native enable flags like Factorio's mod-list.json) while updates re-resolve dependencies, back up changed files, and stay idempotent when nothing has actually changed.

I'm also sketching atomic write semantics—staging files with temp names before renaming them into place, with rollback from backups if anything fails partway—and defining a GuestFs abstraction for file existence checks, reads, writes, renames, removal, listing, and directory creation across the guest filesystem.

For the actual connection, real servers use SSH2 with SFTP, authenticating via a management key with password fallback, while sandbox mode simulates a guest filesystem under a local temp directory keyed by server ID. To discover a server's install layout, I avoid shell commands like `find` in favor of checking candidate paths directly through GuestFs, seeding the sandbox with a fake skeleton (e.g. server.properties under /opt/mc for Minecraft) so discovery logic works identically in both real and sandboxed environments.

For ownership fixes, I only run chown in real mode, building the command from sanitized relative paths that must match a strict allowed character set — rejecting empty segments, ".", "..", or anything outside the safe character range — and if any entry in the package is unsafe, I reject the whole package rather than trying to partially sanitize it.

For the restart requirement, the brief wants a "restart-required" prompt rather than an automatic restart, so I need somewhere to persist that pending state. I'm weighing options like detecting install time versus last server start, using a notification, or storing a flag somewhere, but nothing fits cleanly without touching schema that belongs to another part of the system like game config.

Since adding a field to ServerMod would step into territory I don't own, I'm considering instead computing "restart pending" by comparing Job history — checking if the latest successful mod sync job finished after the last successful power start/restart job, and whether that sync actually changed something that needs a restart.

I'm starting to write the path-safety module, defining a regex for safe filename segments, but reconsidering whether to exclude single quotes since they could complicate shell quoting even though I use proper shell escaping elsewhere.

I'm designing normalizeArchivePath to sanitize zip entry names by converting backslashes to slashes, stripping leading "./", and rejecting absolute paths or ".." traversal segments, plus a joinUnder helper that confirms the resolved path stays within the base directory. Then I'm planning the zip archive reader itself -- locating the end-of-central-directory signature, parsing central directory entries for compression method, encryption flags, and sizes, and rejecting encrypted or zip64 archives that aren't supported.

I also need to reject symlink entries by checking Unix external attributes, locate the local file header to find the data offset, and decompress using zlib's raw inflate with output length limits, verifying the result against the expected uncompressed size and CRC32. Finally I'm setting safety caps on entry count, total uncompressed size, per-entry size, and compression ratio to guard against zip bombs.

Then I'm considering a tar.gz reader for Metamod-style archives, handling 512-byte headers and typeflags, rejecting symlinks and hardlinks, and supporting PAX/GNU longname extensions for path overrides while rejecting other types. I'm weighing whether tar support is actually needed given it's only relevant for certain frameworks, but decide to write a small reader anyway since other plugin ecosystems also ship tar.gz releases.

I'm compiling an allowlist of hosts for a safe-fetch module covering Modrinth, Thunderstore, uMod, Spiget, Hangar, GitHub, Factorio, Ficsit, AlliedMods, and Vintage Story CDNs, and noting that Spigot resource downloads redirect through spigotmc.org behind Cloudflare.

For Spigot, if downloads redirect to an unlisted external host, I'll fail gracefully with a message telling the user to download manually, since Spiget's CDN only covers resources it hosts directly. I need to verify the actual redirect targets for Factorio and Thunderstore downloads via curl before finalizing the implementation using Node's https module.

I'm building a download function that validates resolved IPs against private ranges to prevent DNS rebinding, manually follows redirects up to five hops with revalidation at each step, streams the response while enforcing a byte cap, and computes multiple hash digests concurrently before returning the buffer and hashes for verification against an expected checksum. I also need a smaller JSON-fetching helper that reuses the same host allowlist logic but with a tighter size limit.

For the mirror system, I'm planning that before hitting the upstream source, a lookup checks if the file already exists locally under a verified mirror directory, validating its hash against the expected or mirror-provided checksum and falling back to upstream on mismatch. I'm also sketching out the type definitions for expected hashes, remote file metadata (including mirror source info), and resolved package identifiers.

Now I'm defining the resolution output type, which captures the root package, the full dependency-ordered package list, any incompatible packages that must be excluded, informational notes, and whether a restart is required, along with an error type and the installer context structure.

Continuing on, I'm sketching the FamilyInstaller interface — it defines the layout of guest filesystem paths and starts specifying a detect method that locates the mod loader's directories on the guest and errors out if it isn't present.

I'm designing the guest-side state schema for tracking installed packages, their files with hashes, and which root mods require them, keyed by stable GameMod ids for identity tracking.

For the install operation, I'm working through the conflict resolution logic: checking if a requested package already exists with matching version and files to skip reinstalling, otherwise handling file placement conflicts between packages owned by different mods, overwriting files owned by the same package for repairs, and figuring out how to handle files that already exist but weren't tracked by the system, like something a user manually installed.

I also need to handle incompatibility declarations in both directions — checking the resolution for conflicts against the current state, and checking whether existing packages marked the new one as incompatible. For safety, I should back up any file before overwriting it into a timestamped backup folder, keeping only the most recent five, and writes should be staged to a temp file then renamed atomically. For uninstalling, I need to remove the mod from package roots and delete orphaned files, though I need to be careful about files a user may have edited directly inside a plugin folder.

For disabling a mod, I'll only move the root package's files (leaving dependencies alone since they're harmless if unused), refusing to disable if another enabled root still depends on it, and enabling reverses this with a path conflict check.

Update should share the same apply logic as install — compare versions, back up old files, replace with new ones, and treat any version mismatch as an implicit update rather than a separate code path.

I need to decide on restart requirements (Oxide hot-loads plugins so may not need one) and handle post-write ownership fixes via a reference-directory chown, which is a no-op locally. Now I'm moving into the per-family specifics starting with Minecraft.

For Minecraft, I'm working out directory detection by checking a list of candidate paths for server.properties, pulling the game version from a pinned config or the server log, reading level-name from server.properties, and determining the variant (vanilla/paper/fabric/etc.) to figure out where plugins, mods, and datapacks live relative to the base directory.

Now I'm mapping compatibility rules: datapacks work across any variant, mods/plugins need their loader to match the server variant (with an acceptable-loaders table for each variant like paper accepting paper/spigot/bukkit/datapack), modpacks require matching the pack's underlying loader, and resource packs/shaders are flagged as client-side and unsupported for server installs.

For resolving Modrinth packages, I'm planning to fetch the project's versions filtered by loader and game version, preferring release builds, then determine placement based on the version's loader type -- plugin jar for server loaders, mod jar for fabric/forge-type loaders, datapack zip for datapacks, or an .mrpack file for modpacks. I also need a project-info call to get project_type, title, and server_side fields to guide this placement logic.

I'm working out dependency resolution: required dependencies get recursively resolved via project_id (or the specific version if given), incompatible dependencies get flagged by key as "modrinth:<project_id>", and embedded ones get skipped -- capping at 30 total packages and a recursion depth of 5. For file handling, I'll use the primary file's sha1/sha512 hashes, size, and CDN URL, and keep the upstream filename as-is rather than renaming it, since that's cleaner and safer.

But I need to account for legacy installs that used the old "nxeon-<slug>.jar" naming -- since those files aren't tracked in the new state, updating or removing them would silently leave stale files behind. So I should add legacy file path detection (checking both plugins/ and mods/ directories) so the engine can clean those up during uninstall/update even when they're not in the current state, and this same logic needs to apply across game installers like Valheim too.

For mrpack support, I'm working out how to parse a downloaded .mrpack archive by reading its modrinth.index.json manifest, which lists the format version, game info, file paths with hashes and download URLs, and dependency constraints (Minecraft version, mod loader type). I need to validate that the loader and Minecraft version in the manifest actually match the server's configured variant before proceeding.

I also need to enforce safety: skip files marked unsupported for server environments, sanitize file paths to prevent escaping the install directory, restrict download URLs to an allowlist of trusted Modrinth-related hosts, merge in any "overrides" and "server-overrides" directories (with server-overrides taking priority), and cap the total file count to something reasonable like 500. The resulting package's files will need to be fetched asynchronously when placed.

Since modpacks can be large, place() should accept an async fetcher and I should cap the total download size—maybe 300MB—checked upfront from the index before downloading anything, with a clear error if it's exceeded, to avoid memory issues. I'm also considering that override files might overwrite existing server configs, which needs a backup or confirmation step.

For Spigot, I'm working out the resolve flow: hit the Spiget API for resource metadata, reject external or premium resources, and use the download endpoint which redirects to the CDN jar. Since Spiget doesn't provide hashes, I'll compute sha256 myself, and name the resulting jar `nxeon-<slug>.jar` to maintain compatibility with legacy naming conventions.

For Hangar, I'm resolving versions through the platform-specific API endpoint, extracting download info including the sha256 hash from fileInfo, and handling plugin dependencies by name lookup against Hangar itself since K2's schema references Hangar even though there are no catalog rows for it yet—I'll implement a minimal version to start. Then for Valheim via Thunderstore, detection hinges on checking for the bepinex game variant or the presence of the Valheim directory.

For the lloesche Valheim image, enabling BEPINEX causes it to install BepInEx into /opt/valheim/bepinex and copy plugins from the config directory into it at boot, with an error thrown if the variant isn't set to bepinex. I'm working through the exact directory layout—where plugins live versus where BepInEx config files actually get synced, since I'm not certain lloesche syncs config files the same way it syncs plugins.

Now I'm figuring out how to resolve mod packages via Thunderstore's API: fetching the latest version info (download URL, dependencies, full name) from the experimental endpoint, then recursively resolving each dependency string into its own package lookup, and deciding whether to pin specific dependency versions or just grab the latest, similar to how mod managers like r2modman handle it.

I'm also sorting out which packages to skip -- BepInExPack loader variants since the server already provides the loader -- and wrestling with how patcher-type packages (which install into BepInEx/patchers rather than plugins) should be handled, since I'm not sure the server image syncs that directory from config.

Since Thunderstore's API doesn't expose a reliable hash, I'll just record the sha256 myself and cap file size. For placement, I need to detect the package's internal layout -- files can sit at root, inside a plugins folder, or nested under BepInEx/plugins, config, patchers, or core -- and map each case to the right install path under plugins/<FullName>/.

For Rust, I'm handling Oxide/Carbon detection by checking the plugin directories for each, and if neither framework is present, surfacing an error telling the user to switch server type in settings.

For resolving plugin downloads, I'm looking at the umod.org API endpoint that returns plugin metadata including name and download URL, and figuring out how to parse "Requires:" comments from plugin source headers to resolve dependencies.

Restart isn't needed for Oxide/Carbon since they hot-reload plugins. For cs2, I need to detect the base game directory and require both metamod and counterstrikesharp addons present, erroring out if missing—though I could later make those frameworks installable packages themselves. For resolving cs2 plugins, I'll pull from GitHub releases, picking a zip asset that avoids Windows-specific builds and preferring linux or generic ones, using the sha256 digest GitHub provides for verification.

Now I'm working out the archive normalization logic for placing cs2 plugin files, handling various folder structures like nested addons paths, top-level plugin folders, loose dlls, and shared directories so everything lands correctly under addons/counterstrikesharp.

For restrictions, I'm deciding only files under csgo/addons/counterstrikesharp/** and csgo/cfg/** should be allowed unless the package is explicitly a framework. On restart behavior, since CSS supports hot-reloading plugins by default via its config, I'm leaning toward still marking restartRequired as true for safety.

For the framework-level install of Metamod + CSS together, I'm concerned that the joedwards32 image reruns steamcmd on every startup, which resets gameinfo.gi and breaks Metamod loading. Since I can't verify this on an actual CS2 server, I think it's safer to mark the framework install as not yet supported, while CSS plugin installs still require it.

I'll do a read-only check instead — inspecting the live CS2 server for an addons/metamod directory, plus similar diagnostics on Rust's oxide folder, Valheim's BepInEx dirs, and Minecraft's plugin directories. I'll write a small script using ssh2 with the management credentials to run these checks, keeping everything strictly read-only.

import { SPR, APP } from "@/lib/nx/sprites";
import { NX_ICONS, NX_ICON_TONE, type NxTone } from "@/lib/nx/icon-paths";

/* ── one dial for icon size, site-wide ────────────────────────────────────
   Every mark in the system is drawn a fixed multiple of the size its call site
   asks for. Applying it HERE rather than editing hundreds of call sites keeps
   the relative sizing intact: an icon that was deliberately smaller than its
   neighbour stays proportionally smaller, it is just bigger in absolute terms.
   Change this one number to retune the whole set.

   Note for anyone adding a primitive: scale exactly ONCE per rendered mark.
   `Plate` draws an `Icon` inside itself, so it scales its own BOX and passes
   the raw size through — scaling in both places would compound to 2.25x. */
export const ICON_SCALE = 1.5;
export const iconPx = (n: number) => Math.round(n * ICON_SCALE);

/**
 * One interface mark.
 *
 * VECTOR FIRST, sprite as the fallback. `lib/nx/icon-paths.ts` carries the set
 * redrawn as 24x24 paths; anything it defines renders as an inline SVG in
 * `currentColor`, and anything it doesn't — the sheet's brand row (linux,
 * docker, postgres…) and the five 3D product renders — still comes off
 * `public/nx/nxicons.webp` exactly as before.
 *
 * Why the switch is here rather than at 137 call sites: the sprite's marks are
 * pre-coloured, so one inside a tinted control renders in the SHEET's colour
 * instead of the control's (a teal shieldcheck on a violet "Admin" chip is the
 * bug that started this). Routing both through one component means every call
 * site gets `currentColor` without being edited, and a name with no vector yet
 * silently keeps working.
 *
 * `size` still means what it always did — ICON_SCALE is applied here for BOTH
 * paths, so a swap is 1:1 and `Plate` (which sizes its box with `iconPx`)
 * needs no change.
 */

I should draft docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md, laying out a table with columns for family, mods tab availability, installer, real vs simulated status, catalog size as of the prod snapshot, loader support, and known gaps, covering all 52 game families.

The real vs simulated distinction comes down to ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS=1 being set in the prod env file, which the worker picks up — confirming the real path is what's executing live. Live state showed 11 ServerMod rows (7 MC, 3 Valheim installed, 1 Rust failed due to password-only SSH on a key-only server).

From the audit I'm cataloging the bugs in the old system: the panel only loaded the top 400 rows client-side, hiding most of the 32k MC mods from search; compatibility checks only looked at appliesToVariant, letting Fabric mods get offered on Paper servers and fail on install; the Minecraft installer had no game-version filtering, dependency resolution, checksum verification, or URL allowlisting; Valheim installs skipped BepInEx variant checks and dependency installation while also unzipping manifest files; and the legacy SSH transport's password-only auth breaks on key-only servers, which explains the live Rust failure. I'm now looking into what else went wrong with that live Rust server.

Live Rust servers are vanilla, so nothing actually installs Oxide/Carbon for the oxide variants — it's just a label — meaning uMod installs fail with NODIR, and the same gap exists for CS2's metamod variant where nothing installs Metamod/CSS. There are also 2 live vanilla Valheim servers, and I note that the "INSTALLED" status really just means the config was written, not that the game has fetched the content yet, which is honest enough. I want to check the prod catalog family counts, which sum to roughly 64k, before writing up the docs and updating DOCUMENTATION.md section 15 — I need to locate where that section is.

# One-click mod coverage — every game family (audit + build, 2026-10-01)

Branch `feature/one-click-mod-installers` (agent K1). This file is the honest
map of what the Mods tab can and cannot do for each game we host, and why.
The machine-readable version of the same table is
`lib/mods/installers/index.ts` (`familyCoverage()`), which the worker, the
Mods tab and `test/mods-installers.test.ts` all read — if this file and that
module ever disagree, the module is right and this file is stale.

## 1. What actually runs in production (audit)

- `ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS=1` is set in `/opt/nxeon/.env`, and the worker unit
  (`nxeon-worker.service`) loads that file (`EnvironmentFile=/opt/nxeon/.env`).
  So in production mod changes take the **REAL** path over SSH — nothing is
  simulated. The SANDBOX-only simulation in `worker/game-mods.ts` never runs
  in prod.
- Live state at audit time (read-only prod DB query): 11 `ServerMod` rows —
  7 Minecraft INSTALLED, 3 Valheim INSTALLED, 1 Rust FAILED with
  `All configured authentication methods failed`.
- Catalogue: **64,000+ active GameMod rows** across 41 families/sources (table
  below). The Mods tab, however, loaded only the top **400** rows per game and
  filtered them in the browser — so for Minecraft (32,252 rows) a search could
  only ever find something in the first 400. That, not the catalogue, is why it
  looked like "a tiny curated set".

### Bugs found in the pre-existing installer (fixed on this branch)

| # | Bug | Effect | Fix |
|---|-----|--------|-----|
| 1 | Panel `findMany({ take: 400 })` + client-side search | 99% of the Minecraft catalogue unreachable | DB-side search/filter/sort/paging (`searchModCatalog`) |
| 2 | Compatibility used only `appliesToVariant`; most rows have it null and carry `loaders[]` instead | Fabric/Forge mods offered with an Install button on Paper servers (and vice-versa); install then fetched a "paper" build that doesn't exist | Per-installer compat (`mcCompat` etc.), "Works on this server" filter on by default |
| 3 | Modrinth resolve took `versions[0]` filtered by loader only — **no game-version filter**, no dependencies, no checksum; the VM `curl`ed whatever URL came back | Could install a 1.21.4 jar on a 1.21.1 server; required libraries (e.g. Fabric API) never installed; no integrity check | Version+loader-matched pick, required-dependency walk, `incompatible` honoured, sha1+sha512 verified |
| 4 | Legacy SSH transport (`worker/game-mods.ts withSsh`) was password-only | Fails on servers that only accept the management key — the live Rust FAILED row | New transport (`worker/mods-guest-ssh.ts`) tries the management key first, like `lib/sftp.ts` |
| 5 | Valheim: no check for the BepInEx server type; whole Thunderstore zip (manifest, icon, README) unzipped into `plugins/nxeon-<slug>/`; dependencies ignored | Mods "installed" on vanilla servers that can't load them; missing deps (Jötunn etc.) | Variant gate, Thunderstore layout mapping, dependency walk, BepInExPack skipped, patchers refused |
| 6 | Downloads ran on the VM via `curl` from any URL an API returned | No host allowlist, no size cap, no checksum | Worker-side `safeFetch`: https-only allowlist re-checked per redirect, DNS-pinned private-IP refusal, size cap, hash verification |
| 7 | No uninstall bookkeeping beyond a deterministic filename | Removing a mod left its dependencies; no update/disable | Guest state file with dependency ref-counts; update / disable / enable / uninstall |

### Gaps found that are NOT install-mechanics (owner/other agents)

- **Rust**: the `oxide` / `carbon` server types are labels only — nothing on the
  platform installs Oxide or Carbon (grep: no `RUST_OXIDE_ENABLED` anywhere),
  and both live Rust servers are `vanilla`. The installer now says so plainly
  ("doesn't have Oxide or Carbon installed") instead of failing with NODIR.
  Wiring the variant to the image (`didstopia/rust-server` supports
  `RUST_OXIDE_ENABLED=1`) belongs to game-config (agent R).
- **CS2**: same for `metamod` — nothing installs Metamod:Source or
  CounterStrikeSharp. Plugins install only where both folders already exist.
- **Valheim**: 2 of 4 live servers are `vanilla`; their customers must switch
  to BepInEx (Settings) before mods can load. The panel tells them.
- **Catalogue depth** (agent K2): Rust has only 29 uMod rows (uMod lists
  thousands); 7 Days to Die, V Rising and Bedrock have none.
- I could NOT verify any of this on live guests: a read-only SSH probe of the
  live game servers' mod folders was refused by the session's permission
  classifier ("Production Reads"). See "Needs owner" in the branch report.

## 2. The new installer interface

```
lib/mods/
  types.ts            FamilyInstaller: compat / detect / resolve / place / legacyPaths / configure
  engine.ts           installOrUpdate · uninstall · setDisabled · previewResolve
  safe-fetch.ts       the only network path (allowlist, SSRF guard, size cap, hashes)
  archive.ts          ZIP + tar(.gz) reader: zip-slip/abs/drive/symlink/hardlink refusal, bomb caps, CRC
  paths.ts            segment allowlist, joinUnder, shell quoting
  mirror.ts           NX Labs mirror read (ModVersion.mirrorPath, re-hashed) → else upstream
  guest-fs.ts         GuestFs + LocalGuestFs (tests + SANDBOX fake guest)
  queue.ts            ServerMod status flip + GAME_MOD_SYNC under the per-server lock
  facts.ts            DB rows → CatalogFacts / ServerFacts
  installers/
    minecraft.ts      Modrinth (plugins/mods/datapacks/.mrpack), Hangar, SpigotMC
    valheim.ts        Thunderstore → BepInEx plugins
    rust.ts           uMod .cs (+ // Requires:)
    cs2.ts            CounterStrikeSharp plugins from GitHub releases
    factorio.ts       mods.factorio.com (+ mod-list.json)
    index.ts          coverage table for all 52 families
worker/mods-guest-ssh.ts   real GuestFs over one SSH connection (key → password)
worker/game-mods.ts        GAME_MOD_SYNC: engine families first, legacy families unchanged
```

Per operation the engine: detects the real folder and game version on the
server → resolves the build + required dependencies from the source → downloads
(mirror first, checksum-verified) → maps files with the safe archive reader →
refuses if a target exists that Nxeon didn't install, or a declared
incompatible mod is present → backs up anything it will overwrite or delete to
`/root/.nxeon-mods/backups/<stamp>-<slug>/` (newest 5 kept) → writes each file
as `<name>.nxeon-part` then renames → records exactly what it wrote in
`/root/.nxeon-mods/state.json` → rolls everything back if any write fails.
Re-running an install that is already current downloads nothing and changes
nothing. Disable moves files to `/root/.nxeon-mods/disabled/` (Factorio uses its
own `mod-list.json` flag). Uninstall removes a dependency only when no other
installed mod needs it. Result + restart flag go on the job row
(`payload.result`), which drives the Mods tab's "Restart to load your changes".

ServerMod statuses (plain String column — **no schema change**): resting
`INSTALLED | DISABLED | FAILED`; pending `INSTALLING | UPDATING | DISABLING |
ENABLING | REMOVING`.

## 3. Coverage table

Catalogue sizes are active, upstream-OK rows in production on 2026-10-01.
"Mods tab" is yes for every family: the tab always shows the catalogue; where
there's no installer it shows each mod's source link + the reason, never an
Install button.

| Family | Installer | Real vs simulated | Catalogue (source: rows) | Loader / mechanism | Gaps |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| minecraft | **engine** (new) | real over SSH; SANDBOX runs the same pipeline on a fake guest dir | modrinth 32,243 · spigotmc 7 · github 2 (not installable) | Paper/Purpur/Spigot plugins → `plugins/`; Fabric/Quilt/Forge/NeoForge mods → `mods/`; datapacks → `<level>/datapacks`; `.mrpack` modpacks (server files + server-overrides, exact loader+version match, ≤600 files / 400 MB) | NeoForge/Quilt aren't offered as server types in Settings yet; Hangar resolver ready but no Hangar rows yet (K2) |
| valheim | **engine** (new) | real | thunderstore 1,238 | BepInEx plugins → `/opt/valheim/config/bepinex/plugins/<Author-Name>/` (image syncs on start) | needs BepInEx server type; packages with `patchers/`/`core/` refused (preloader not synced by the image) |
| rust | **engine** (new) | real — but no live server has Oxide | umod 29 · codefling 1 (not installable) | uMod `.cs` → `oxide/plugins` or `carbon/plugins`, hot-loaded, `// Requires:` deps | Oxide/Carbon not installed by the platform (agent R); catalogue thin (K2) |
| cs2 | **engine** (new) | real — only where Metamod + CSS already exist | github 22 · steam_workshop 991 (maps; not installable) | CounterStrikeSharp plugins → `csgo/addons/counterstrikesharp/{plugins,shared,configs}`, sha256 digest when GitHub publishes it | No one-click Metamod/CSS framework install (gameinfo.gi edit unverified); Workshop maps need `host_workshop_map` launch args |
| factorio | **engine** (new) | real — needs the owner's factorio.com token | factorio_portal 5,446 | portal zip → `/opt/factorio/mods` + `mod-list.json`; deps with `!`/`?`/`~` + version constraints; sha1 verified | Wube requires a factorio.com username+token for downloads; read from `config/server-settings.json` on the server, never stored |
| terraria | legacy (TShock) | real, live-verified 2026-09-30 | github 23 | TShock `.dll` → restart → confirmed in TShock's log, else rolled back | — |
| ark | legacy | real (config-write; game downloads) | steam_workshop 1,000 | `GAME_MOD_IDS` env | — |
| unturned | legacy | real | steam_workshop 1,000 | `WorkshopDownloadConfig.json` | — |
| dst | legacy | real | steam_workshop 1,000 | `MODS` env | — |
| squad | legacy | real | steam_workshop 272 | `MODS` env | — |
| soulmask | legacy | real | steam_workshop 678 | `MOD_IDS` env | — |
| projectzomboid | legacy | real | steam_workshop 1,000 | `WorkshopItems=` + `Mods=` | — |
| tf2 | legacy | real, gated on a Workshop auth key | steam_workshop 1,000 | `tf_workshop_map_sync` | no auth key provisioned → honest failure |
| l4d2 | legacy | real | steam_workshop 1,000 | steamcmd → `addons/*.vpk` | image layout inferred (see 2026-09-20 entry) |
| empyrion | legacy | real | steam_workshop 1,000 | one scenario → `CustomScenario` | one at a time |
| kf2 | legacy | real, live-verified | steam_workshop 1,000 | `ServerSubscribedWorkshopItems` | — |
| gmod | legacy | real, live-verified | steam_workshop 999 | steamcmd → gmad extract → `addons/` | — |
| necesse | legacy | real, live-verified | steam_workshop 521 | steamcmd → `mods/*.jar` | — |
| vintagestory | legacy | real, live-verified | vintagestory_moddb 3,934 | ModDB → `data/Mods` + modinfo deps | — |
| armareforger | legacy | real | reforger_workshop 198 | `MODS_JSON_B64` → `game.mods` | — |
| satisfactory | legacy | real | ficsit 923 | ficsit.app LinuxServer → `FactoryGame/Mods` (+SML) | — |
| palworld | unavailable | — | steam_workshop 1,000 · nexus 12 | Workshop is Windows-server-only; pak/UE4SS on Linux unverified | manual upload to `Pal/Content/Paks/~mods` |
| conan | unavailable | — | steam_workshop 992 | needs a verified modlist.txt path on the wine image | — |
| dayz | unavailable | — | steam_workshop 899 | needs a logged-in Steam account + `-mod=` | — |
| barotrauma | unavailable | — | steam_workshop 1,000 | content packages need a verified config edit | — |
| stationeers | unavailable | — | steam_workshop 999 | not wired | — |
| spaceengineers | unavailable | — | mod_io 1,170 · steam_workshop 998 | not wired for the Linux server | — |
| corekeeper / eco / mordhau / sandstorm | unavailable | — | mod_io 194 / 159 / 801 / 560 | mod.io needs a per-game API key | — |
| sonsoftheforest / sunkenland / schedule1 | unavailable | — | thunderstore 73 / 22 / 438 | server images ship no BepInEx; Schedule I has no dedicated server | — |
| cs16 | unavailable | — | github 9 | AMXX plugins need per-server compile | — |
| sdtd, vrising, enshrouded, theforest, bedrock, dragonwilds, abioticfactor, icarus, arkasa, nightingale, theisle, plutonium×4, ets2, ats | unavailable | — | 0 | see `COVERAGE_UNAVAILABLE` reasons | catalogue + mechanism both missing |

## 4. Verification done (and not done)

- `test/mods-installers.test.ts`: archive safety against real ZIP/tar bytes
  (zip-slip, absolute, drive-letter, symlink, encrypted, duplicate, CRC, bomb),
  download guard (allowlist, raw IP, creds, ports, private ranges, checksum),
  mirror path containment, every installer's pure placement logic against the
  real archive layouts of each ecosystem, and the engine end-to-end on a
  temp-dir guest: install with dependency → idempotent re-run (no download) →
  disable/enable → update (old file removed) → uninstall (orphaned dependency
  removed), plus conflict-with-hand-installed-file, declared incompatibility,
  legacy-file replacement and checksum-mismatch-installs-nothing.
- NOT verified on a live game server (no live test VMs in this task; read-only
  SSH probing was refused). The first real install per engine family should be
  watched by a human.

content.content:
---

*Companion docs: `CLAUDE.md` (agent/ops conventions), `ROADMAP.md` (backlog), `docs/MIGRATION.md`
(server migration).*
> effect."*

The comment at `:71-85` records what it replaced: production had no flag, so every real customer
request fell through, stamped an `_appliedAt` marker, and notified *"Game settings applied on
`<hostname>`"* with the `(sandbox)` qualifier suppressed — because `SANDBOX` is false on production.
The customer changed their difficulty or slot count and was told it was applied.

So the lie is gone, but **the feature is non-functional today** and the customer-facing copy has not
caught up: `components/customer/GameSettings.tsx:73` says *"Changes are queued and applied to the
server"* and `:127` says *"Settings queued for apply."* Even on the real path, nothing reads back —
`worker/game-config.ts:118-165` writes files over SSH and notifies "applied" without confirming the
write landed or the service restarted, and `:138-145` writes the `_appliedAt` marker even when
`outcome.ok === false`.

**2. Auto-update used to be unable to fail — closed.** The remote command was
`set -e; ${steam}${restart}; true`: the steamcmd update was `|| true` and skipped entirely if
`steamcmd` was absent, every restart branch was `|| true`, and the whole command ended `; true`. It
**could not exit non-zero**, so for every server with `autoUpdate: true` the handler always resolved
and always fired *"The latest server update was applied and the service was restarted"* — unattended,
every 6 hours, regardless of what actually happened on the box.

The command builder, the output parser and the verdict now live in
`/opt/nxeon/lib/game-update-verify.ts`, and the design rules are stated where they can be enforced
(`:60-77`):

- **No `set -e`, no trailing `; true`, no `|| true`.** Control flow is explicit and the exit status is
  irrelevant — **the markers are the contract** (`updateCommand`, `:78`), so a truncated or dropped
  connection is detectable by the absence of `NXGU:END` rather than indistinguishable from success.
- **steamcmd's own exit code is not trusted** — it is unreliable and frequently non-zero on a
  perfectly good update — so its success line is matched instead and the code reported alongside.
- *"No unit matched"* is an outcome that gets emitted, not a branch that gets swallowed.
- The post-restart state is polled and reported verbatim; `active` is the only thing called success.

`parseGameUpdateOutput` (`:163`) and `judgeGameUpdate` (`:213`) turn that into a verdict.
`worker/game-update.ts:145` throws on `!verdict.ok`, which puts the reason in `Job.error` and the
admin job list, and the success notification at `:160` uses the verdict's own title and body. Guarded
by `test/game-update.test.ts`.

## Build with AI — Claude Code on every VPS

content.thinking:
I'm noticing the segment regex rejects legitimate leading dots like ".nxeon-mods" or ".github", so I need to allow a leading dot while still blocking "." and ".." as whole segments. I also need to allow "$" for Java inner class names, since shell quoting with single quotes handles that safely.

But for jar/datapack validation, I realize we never actually extract paths — we just treat the archive as one file — so enforcing strict path rules there is pointless. Better to write a lightweight `isValidZipContainer` check that just confirms the EOCD and central directory structure parse correctly without inflating entries, and reserve the strict path validation for formats we actually extract and inspect, like mrpack, Thunderstore, CSS, and Factorio.

For Factorio specifically, since we only need to read info.json and place the zip as-is, I want a lenient listing approach rather than full strict parsing, since mod names can include unicode locale files that strict normalization would reject. I'm thinking of a `readZip` option that skips path normalization and only inflates entries matching a filter function, so Factorio mods just extract info.json lazily.

For the allowed-character set used in strict extraction cases, I'll loosen it slightly to include `$` and leading dots, while still excluding unicode and apostrophes since those are rare edge cases not worth the risk.

input.description: Add lenient zip mode and widen segment allowlist

The Rust re-run showing changed=1 is odd given the results look good otherwise—I'm trying to figure out why, maybe it's the legacy path resolution for Rust returning a different directory than expected.

Actually I found the real bug: the legacy-path filter doesn't exclude files already owned by current state, so on re-run the engine thinks the existing Vanish.cs is an orphaned legacy file and would delete it even though it just wrote it. The Jotunn and Valheim pdb/mdb checks look fine, so I'll focus on applying this one fix.
