entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

#!/bin/bash
# Global lock so only ONE heavy job (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) runs at a time on
# this box. This machine is the live production primary (also hosts ~40 customer VMs, swap is
# nearly full) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers can OOM or starve production.
# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
exec flock -w 3600 /tmp/nxeon-heavy.lock nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"

1	#!/bin/bash
2	# Two-slot lock so at most TWO heavy jobs (tsc, next dev, playwright, test suites) run at once on this box.
3	# This machine is the live production primary (also hosts customer VMs) — uncontrolled parallel tsc/dev servers
4	# can OOM or starve production. (Was 1 slot; raised to 2 on 2026-10-01 because 20 agents were queueing.)
5	# usage: heavy.sh bash -c "cd /opt/nxeon-wt-foo && npx tsc --noEmit -p ."
6	deadline=$((SECONDS + 3600))
7	while [ $SECONDS -lt $deadline ]; do
8	  for i in 1 2; do
9	    exec {fd}>/tmp/nxeon-heavy.$i.lock
10	    if flock -n $fd; then
11	      exec nice -n 19 ionice -c3 env NODE_OPTIONS="--max-old-space-size=3072" "$@"
12	    fi
13	    exec {fd}>&-
14	  done
15	  sleep 2
16	done
17	echo "heavy.sh: timed out waiting for a slot" >&2; exit 75

input.message:
K1 modinstall: branch `feature/one-click-mod-installers`, worktree `/opt/nxeon-wt-modinstall`. Commits f1823272c2, d98333994c, 05f11be5dd, all pushed by the hook. Typecheck is clean and 41/41 tests pass. The Mods tab UI was never rendered successfully, and nothing was run on a live game server. Note: /root/agent-notes/modinstall.md.

**What I found (full table for all 52 families in `docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md`)**
- Production really installs: `ENABLE_REAL_GAMEMODS=1` is set and the worker loads that env file.
- The Mods tab only ever loaded the top 400 catalogue rows and searched them in the browser. That's why Minecraft (32k mods) looked like a tiny curated set.
- Compatibility only looked at `appliesToVariant`, so Fabric mods showed an Install button on Paper servers.
- The Minecraft installer had no game-version filter, no dependencies and no checksum, and the VM curled any URL an API returned.
- Valheim installs didn't check for the BepInEx server type.
- The old SSH connection used the password only. That's why the one live Rust install failed ("All configured authentication methods failed").
- Rust `oxide`/`carbon` and CS2 `metamod` server types are labels only: nothing installs those frameworks. Rust has only 29 uMod rows.

**What changed**
- `lib/mods/`: one shared install engine. Downloads come only from listed https hosts (re-checked on every redirect), private IPs are refused, size is capped and sha1/sha256/sha512 are checked. It reads from the NX Labs mirror first via raw SQL, so it works before or after K2's ModVersion table exists. The archive reader refuses zip-slip, absolute paths, symlinks, hardlinks and zip bombs. It resolves dependencies and refuses declared conflicts. It never overwrites a file Nxeon didn't install. It backs up to `/root/.nxeon-mods/backups`, rolls back on failure, and records what it wrote in `/root/.nxeon-mods/state.json` on the server. Re-running a current install changes nothing. Install, update, disable/enable and uninstall all work.
- Installers in `lib/mods/installers/`:
  - Minecraft: Modrinth plugins, mods, datapacks and modpacks; Hangar; Spigot.
  - Valheim: Thunderstore to BepInEx.
  - Rust: uMod.
  - CS2: CounterStrikeSharp from GitHub.
  - Factorio: the mod portal; it needs the owner's factorio.com token in `server-settings.json`.
- Older working paths (Workshop games, TShock, Vintage Story, Satisfactory, Reforger) are unchanged. Families with no real mechanism show a plain "not yet available" reason and no Install button.
- `worker/game-mods.ts` sends the five families above through the engine. It adds the statuses UPDATING, DISABLING, ENABLING and DISABLED, writes job step/progress plus a restart-needed flag, and audit-logs every outcome.
- `worker/mods-guest-ssh.ts` connects with the management key first, then the password.
- `lib/actions-mod-installs.ts` (new) does database-side search and paging over the whole catalogue, a per-server compatibility badge, a dependency preview and an update check. Changes are queued under the per-server lock (`lib/mods/queue.ts`).
- `ModsPanel.tsx` is rewritten on top of this: progress bar, "Restart to load your changes" prompt, installed list with update/disable/remove.

**Verification**
- Unit tests use real archive bytes, including attack shapes, and run the engine end to end.
- `scripts/verify-mod-installers.ts` installed and cleanly uninstalled 7 real mods (LuckPerms; Ledger plus its 2 Fabric dependencies; Terralith; AutoRepair; Jotunn; Vanish; CS2-SimpleAdmin) into a temp fake server. This caught two real bugs, both fixed.
- A sandbox worker run on a throwaway DB went through install → refuse duplicate → disable → enable → update with nothing new → honest failure → Valheim install, all correct.
- The throwaway DB and role are dropped, and the dev server is stopped with `.next` removed.

**Not done / risks**
1. The Playwright screenshots are unusable: the "How did you hear about us?" popup covered the page. The UI was never actually seen; re-run with a Skip click first.
2. No live-server test. The first real install in each of the five families should be watched by someone.
3. Valheim packages that need BepInEx patchers are refused, because I couldn't confirm the server image loads them.
4. No schema change. I'd like these on ServerMod (K2's area): `files Json`, `versionId`, `sha256`, `restartPending`.

**Needs owner**
- The read-only SSH probe of live servers' mod folders was denied ("Production Reads"). I'd want the owner to run it read-only to confirm the folder paths.

**Files edited outside my area**
- `lib/mod-install-support.ts`: adds cs2/github, factorio/factorio_portal and minecraft/hangar. Marketing pages that read this will now count CS2 and Factorio as one-click.
- `lib/game-mods.ts`: customer-facing mod copy updated.
- `lib/actions-mods.ts`: NX Labs install/uninstall now go through the shared queue.
- `test/terraria-plugins.test.ts`: assertion updated for cs2/github.

**Incident**
- I once ran `pkill -f "^bash.*retry \$i"`, a pattern kill, which memory says never to do on this box. The pattern was narrow and nothing else visibly matched, but flag it.

content.text:
I sent my report to the main thread. The installer engine, the per-game installers and the rebuilt Mods tab are committed on `feature/one-click-mod-installers`. The typecheck is clean and all 41 unit tests pass. Two gaps remain: I never actually saw the new Mods tab, and nothing was tried on a live game server.

**What I found:**
- Production really does install mods; nothing is simulated.
- The Mods tab only ever loaded the top 400 catalogue entries and searched those in the browser. That's why Minecraft, with about 32,000 mods, looked like a tiny curated set.
- The old Minecraft install ignored the server's game version, skipped dependencies and never checked file integrity.
- The one failed live Rust install happened because the old SSH connection only tried the root password, never the management key.
- The Rust "Oxide/Carbon" and CS2 "Metamod" server types are labels only: nothing actually installs those frameworks, so mods can't load on those servers yet.

**What's built:**
- **Install engine:** downloads are checked and size-capped, dependencies are resolved, and files Nxeon didn't install are never overwritten. Anything changed is backed up on the server and rolled back if a write fails. Install, update, disable/enable and uninstall all work.
- **Five games on the new path:** Minecraft (plugins, mods, datapacks, modpacks), Valheim, Rust, CS2 and Factorio. Factorio needs the server owner's factorio.com token. The older working installs (Steam Workshop games, Terraria and a few others) are unchanged.
- **Every other game** shows its catalogue with a plain "not yet available" reason and no Install button.
- **Mods tab:** searches the whole catalogue, shows whether each mod fits this server and what dependencies it will pull in, and tracks install progress. It also prompts for a restart when one is needed.
- **Coverage table:** `docs/MODS-COVERAGE.md` covers all 52 games.

**How it was checked:** I installed and cleanly uninstalled 7 real mods into a fake server folder, which caught two bugs that are now fixed. I also ran the worker end to end in sandbox against a throwaway database, and the install, disable, enable, update and honest-failure cases all behaved correctly.
